newsitem.title: FRANCE: Three jailed for killing Algeria settlers' leader.
newsitem.headline: Three jailed for killing Algeria settlers' leader.

text.p: A court sentenced three French far rightists to jail terms of 15 and 20 years on Wednesday for the 1993 murder of the leader of French settlers in Algeria during its war of independence from France.

Jean-Claude Lozano and Gerald Huntz were sentenced to 20 years' jail and Marcel Navarro to 15 years by a court in the southern city of Montpellier for the shooting of Jacques Roseau, the head of the largest group representing settlers.

About 50 riot police guarded the court building as the sentence against the three was read out. Each had claimed innocence, blaming the other two. Huntz initially confessed to the killing but later retracted.
One million French settlers, known as "pieds noirs" (black feet), left Algeria when it gained independence in 1962 after a bloody war and the settlers' movement splintered amid bitter recriminations.

Roseau, 55 and head of the Recours-France settlers' group, was hit in the head and chest by three bullets in March 1993 in his car in Montpellier. His secretary, travelling with him, was lightly wounded.

The three sentenced on Wednesday were members or sympathisers of the far-right settlers' group USDIFRA, which accused Roseau of betrayal for supporting the neo-Gaullist Rally for the Republic Party (RPR) of President Jacques Chirac.
The USDIFRA detests any politics smacking of Gaullism, saying 1960s French leader Charles de Gaulle abandoned their cause and forced them to leave Algeria.

"These very severe sentences prove that the jury realised the danger behind this crime. This danger is the extreme right, whose first victim in France was Jacques Roseau," said Gilbert Collard, a lawyer for Roseau's cousin.
"This verdict...proves that little fascists will not make the law in France," he said.
Outside the court building, supporters of the convicted three protested peacefully.

"They should have been acquitted," said USDIFRA regional leader Emile Vella. "This murder was a sequel to the Algerian war. The three accused have already been punished by three years in prison. That was enough."
In final pleas to the court, the three had protested their innocence and expressed sorrow over the killing. Navarro, saying he would soon be aged 64, pleaded for time with his grandchildren.
